My background combines a PhD in Theoretical Physics with two decades of experience in applied mathematics, software engineering, machine learning, and technical leadership. I believe successful AI systems are built not only on strong models, but on robust architecture, reliable infrastructure, and well-designed engineering processes.

docs.title: Cost-Driven Infrastructure
docs.text: Why renting GPUs often turns out to be excessive, and how to design a payment model with Infracost

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A typical task looks like this: an ML platform team gets a budget and, to avoid depending on capacity availability, rents a GPU cluster for a year. The decision seems reasonable: the hourly price is lower than on-demand, there are no queues, the engineers are calm, and the cost has been forecast and included in the budget. Six months later someone from audit sees that the cluster is busy about a third of the time, and the rest of the time the nodes sit powered on, train nothing, and cost exactly the same. The bill covers every hour of the month, while useful work was done in only some of them.

Nobody in this story made a technical mistake. The cluster is configured correctly, jobs run, models train. The mistake is architectural: infrastructure cost was treated as a fixed line in the budget, not as a function of the real workload profile. We are used to designing reliability through SLAs, redundancy and fault tolerance, and security through threat models and access control. Cost, too often, remains a side effect that is discovered after the fact.

I suggest treating cost as a designed property of the system. The thesis is simple: GPU load during model training is fundamentally uneven, so renting capacity permanently under long commitments is, in most cases, needlessly expensive. It is better to plan no further than a month ahead, commit only to the minimum necessary baseline, and buy peaks on demand. The decision is made by calculation, not by intuition, and the calculation runs on infrastructure described as code. Infrastructure is managed through controlled changes, so we always have a baseline for calculating cost and for controlling cost changes retrospectively. Infracost is one of the most popular tools for this kind of control.

I call this approach cost-driven infrastructure, and the process of revising cost and its forecast should become as regular a project process as tech-debt assessment or metric-drift control.

docs.title: Why GPUs Sit Idle
docs.text:
Model development is not like running a web service with a more or less smooth stream of requests. It is a "data - experiment - evaluation - debugging" cycle, and each phase needs compute capacity to a different degree. Data preparation and cleaning run mostly on CPU and require first of all storage volume. An experiment needs a GPU, but only for the duration of the run itself. Then comes evaluating results, analyzing errors and fixing code, and for all that time the expensive accelerators do nothing. Before a release, demand jumps: several variants must run at once, metrics must be rechecked, training must be repeated on corrected data. After the release, things go quiet again.

This picture is supported not only by practice but also by public research. A team at Shanghai AI Lab analyzed traces from the Acme clusters, which run 4,704 A100 GPUs, and described them in a paper published at NSDI 2024 [1]. Median GPU utilization in LLM development jobs was very high, about 99%, but the load distribution is bimodal: accelerators are either almost fully busy or almost idle, as happens during model evaluation and debugging. The same paper notes that network adapters are idle more than 60% of the time. In other words, "average load" describes such a system poorly, because it has no typical state. There are two extreme modes, and the system switches between them.

The second observation concerns job size. The authors of SAKURAONE, who describe workload dynamics in a single-tenant LLM development environment, show that large jobs use GPUs well, while small jobs on one or two nodes have a median utilization of only 17–23% [2]. They also give a figure that should make us stop and think: canceled jobs account for 73.5% of all occupied GPU time. This does not mean cancellation is always a mistake. For a researcher, stopping a failed experiment quickly is exactly the right thing to do. But the infrastructure pays for it, and pays at a rate calculated for useful work.

A third example shows that even a busy GPU is not always doing useful work. According to a Backblaze publication based on Adobe's data, at first profiling about two thirds of GPU time went to waiting for data [3]. After the input pipeline was optimized, utilization rose to about 80%, which is close to the practical ceiling. That is a separate topic, solved by engineering inside the pipeline rather than by purchasing capacity, but it is a reminder to measure utilization before deciding to buy capacity.

This leads to a practical distinction between two modes. Large pretraining runs occupy many nodes for long periods without pauses, their utilization is high, and long commitments can be justified for them. Small experimental jobs, by contrast, are short, irregular and often canceled, and their utilization is low. These two modes cannot be paid for in the same way. If we buy round-the-clock capacity for experimental work, we pay the "continuous operation" rate for work that is never continuous.

docs.title: Three Ways to Pay for GPUs
docs.text:
To reason about a mixed model, we need a clear view of the payment options. I will use AWS as the best-documented case. Other providers work similarly, with different names.

On-demand. Hourly payment with no commitment. This is the most expensive rate per hour, but also the most flexible: a node starts when needed and stops costing money once it is stopped. The main limitation is not price but availability. Plain on-demand gives no guarantee that the required number of top-tier GPUs will be found at the right moment in the right region.

Short-term reservation. In AWS this is Capacity Blocks for ML. A block can be booked for one to 14 days, or for a period in multiples of seven days up to 182 days, and booking is possible up to eight weeks in advance [4]. Payment is made at booking time, a block cannot be canceled, and up to 64 instances are available in one block. The P4d, P4de, P5, P5e, P5en and P6 families are supported. The price depends on demand, is published per accelerator-hour, and usually sits between on-demand and a one-year reservation [5]. The main advantage of a block is that it guarantees availability for a specific window, which is exactly the problem on-demand does not solve. Many other providers have an analogue in the form of monthly committed plans.

Long-term commitments. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans for one or three years. The provider gives a discount in exchange for your paying for the capacity whether you use it or not. For p4d.24xlarge in us-east-1 with a one-year reservation and no upfront payment, price aggregators give a reference of about $13.92 per hour, which is roughly a 37% discount to on-demand [6].

Check prices against the official price list

The reservation prices in this article come from aggregators and refer to 2026. They are a reference for illustrating the method, not data for a budget. Before planning a purchase, check the figures against the provider's current official price list and verify the terms of the specific plan.

Here are the three options in one table.

Criterion On-demand Short-term reservation Long-term commitment (1–3 years) Price per hour Highest Between on-demand and a one-year reservation Lowest Flexibility Full Limited to the booking window Low Availability guarantee None Yes, for the block period Depends on the reservation type Planning horizon Not needed Days and weeks, up to 8 weeks ahead Years Underuse risk Practically none You pay for the whole block, no cancellation You pay for the whole term regardless of load

The table shows that cheap and flexible never come together, and they are two sides of the same coin. So the question is not "which rate" but "which part of the load to which rate". It can only be answered by calculation, and calculation needs a convenient tool.

docs.title: Cost as Code: Infracost
docs.text:
If infrastructure is described in Terraform, its cost can be calculated before it is applied. This is the task Infracost solves [7]. It reads the configuration code, finds resources, requests prices from the provider and produces a monthly estimate broken down by resource. This turns "how much will it cost" from a guess into a verifiable number that you can get at review time, not at the end of the month.

Here is a minimal example: one node with eight A100 GPUs.

resource "aws_instance" "train_node" {
  ami           = var.dlami_id
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"

  tags = {
    team    = "nlp-research"
    project = "ranker-v3"
    env     = "training"
  }
}

For this configuration, Infracost returns an on-demand estimate of $21.96 per hour, or $16,029 per month at 730 hours. Storage, network and other resources are counted as separate lines. For reference, here are the prices of several GPU instances obtained the same way (AWS, us-east-1, Linux, 730 hours per month).

Instance GPU $/hour $/month p5.48xlarge 8× H100 55.04 40,179 p4d.24xlarge 8× A100 40 GB 21.96 16,029 g5.12xlarge 4× A10G 5.67 4,141 g6.12xlarge 4× L4 4.60 3,359 g5.xlarge 1× A10G 1.01 734

Running it in CI comes down to one command.

infracost scan

The practical value is not in the number itself but in where it appears. If you run the scan in CI, every pull request shows the cost delta: a change that adds two more p4d nodes will show the bill growth right in the code discussion, while it can still be rejected. On top of this, Infracost supports budgets and policies that can block a change if it goes beyond acceptable limits. Tags let you split costs by team and project, which we will need at the end of the month to compare plan and actual.

The current version of Infracost calculates on-demand rates. Reservation and Capacity Blocks prices come from the provider's price lists, not from the tool's estimate. Older versions let you specify reservations through a usage file [8], but I would not rely on that for a mixed scheme. So the "baseline plus peaks" calculation is done on top of the Infracost estimate: the hourly on-demand price comes from the tool, the commitment price from the provider's price list, and the arithmetic itself is done in a simple spreadsheet or a small script. This is not a flaw in the approach but a division of responsibility: Infracost handles what it knows well, namely resource descriptions and current rates, and the decision on commitment structure stays with a person.

docs.title: The "Baseline Plus Peaks" Model
docs.text:
The core of this method fits in one formula. For each node, we need to find out whether it is cheaper to hold it under a commitment or to take it on demand. A commitment costs a fixed amount for the whole month, while on-demand costs in proportion to hours used. So there is a utilization threshold below which the commitment loses. Call it the break-even utilization:

u* = commitment_price / on-demand_price

Both prices are per hour. If a node is needed for more than u of the month, it is cheaper to take it under a commitment. If less, it is cheaper to take it on demand and pay only for the hours actually used. For p4d.24xlarge we get 13.92 / 21.96 ≈ 63%. The threshold is set by prices, not by the size of our team: the bigger the commitment discount, the lower u, and the sooner a reservation starts to pay off. With a 37% discount, a node must be loaded almost two thirds of the time to avoid overpaying.

Consider an end-to-end example. Suppose a team needs one p4d.24xlarge node all the time: regular fine-tuning and serving of experimental models take 730 hours a month. A second node is needed about 200 hours a month for large weekly runs. Two more nodes are needed 100 hours a month each for peak experiments before a release. The actual demand is 730 + 200 + 100 + 100 = 1,130 node-hours per month, and peak simultaneous demand is four nodes. Consider four ways to do it.

Scenario Composition Cost per month A. "Rent with headroom" 4 nodes on-demand 24/7: 4 × 16,029 $64,116 B. "Reserve everything" 4 nodes on a one-year commitment: 4 × 10,162 $40,648 C. "On-demand only when needed" 1,130 h × 21.96 $24,812 D. "Baseline plus peaks" 1 node on commitment ($10,162) + 400 hours on-demand (400 × 21.96 = $8,783) $18,945

The hourly rate in the tables is rounded to the cent; the totals are calculated from the exact Infracost rate. Scenario A is the simplest organizationally and the most expensive. Scenario B lowers the price of an hour, but its utilization is 1,130 / 2,920 = 39%, well below the threshold u*: we pay for three nodes that sit idle for most of the month. Scenario C looks attractive, but it demands strict shutdown discipline and carries the risk that no on-demand nodes will be available at the moment of a peak.

Scenario D gives a total cost estimate of $18,945 and is 53% cheaper than B and 70% cheaper than A. But the most interesting comparison is with C: the mixed scheme is cheaper even than "ideal" on-demand, by about $5,900 a month. The reason is that the baseline node is 100% loaded and clears the threshold u* ≈ 63% with room to spare, so for it a commitment beats hourly payment. The second node is loaded 200 / 730 ≈ 27%, which is below the threshold, so reserving it does not pay. The right decision here is therefore one node in the baseline and the rest on demand. This is not a general rule of "reserve a third". It is the result of a calculation on a specific load profile and specific prices. If prices change or the profile shifts, the answer may change, which is why the calculation should be repeated regularly.

docs.title: Monthly Planning
docs.text:
The model only works when its inputs are kept current. So I recommend using a monthly cycle with three roles: the architect, who owns the structure of the solution and the calculation; FinOps or the finance director, who owns the budget and commitment terms; and the ML team leads, who know their planned hardware load. The principles of FinOps, that is, shared responsibility of engineering, finance and the business for cloud spend, are well described in the FinOps Framework [9], and this approach is essentially its application to GPU workloads.

The cycle consists of five steps.

First: each team sends its training calendar for the month: which runs are planned, how many nodes are needed and for how many hours. Precision to the hour is not needed; an honest estimate is enough, along with the acknowledgment that some runs may not happen.

Second: the architect prepares two or three Terraform variants, for example "baseline only" and "baseline plus peaks", and runs them through Infracost to estimate cost.

Third: based on the results, a decision is made on commitments: how many nodes to move into the baseline and whether to change existing commitments.

Fourth: peaks are booked in advance. If large runs are known weeks ahead, it makes sense to order Capacity Blocks or request quotas, rather than waiting until the nodes are needed urgently.

Fifth: at the end of the month the plan is compared with actuals by tags, and the discrepancies become input for the next cycle.

So that "peaks on demand" does not turn into manual work, you need a mechanism that makes this mode automatic. In practice this is a job queue with autoscaling: Kubernetes with Karpenter, which brings up nodes for queued pods and shuts them down when the work is done, or Slurm with an elastic pool. Then engineers do not need to remember to shut things down, and the baseline configuration is simply always used first, and only the overflow goes to the on-demand configuration. Without such automation, scenario C from the example above stays theoretical: money is saved only if the extra nodes really do shut down.

Roles matter more here than tools. If the architect calculates but has no authority over purchasing, the calculation remains a reference note. If FinOps buys commitments without a load profile, the result is scenario B. If team leads do not send their plans, the baseline is set from last month, and we are always one step behind. A regular cycle is needed precisely so that these three parties regularly synchronize their plans and decisions.

docs.title: Limitations and Risks
docs.text:
The approach has limits, and they are worth keeping in mind.

First: on-demand GPU availability is not guaranteed, especially for top-tier accelerators. A scenario in which peaks depend entirely on whether free nodes can be found at the moment of the request carries a real risk of missed deadlines. So important peaks are better covered by short-term reservations, leaving on-demand for the less critical part of the load.

Second: prices change. In 2026 AWS raised Capacity Blocks prices: by about 15% in January, and then several more times during the year [5]. So the threshold u* is not a constant, and a calculation made six months ago may give the wrong answer. The figures in this article should also be seen as an illustration for a specific moment in time and must be re-checked before a project starts.

Third: GPUs are not the only cost item. Storage for datasets and checkpoints, network traffic, and egress when moving data between regions or outside also cost money, and in some projects they are comparable to compute. Optimizing one item while ignoring the others gives deceptive savings, so the calculation should include all the infrastructure, not just the GPUs.

Fourth: long continuous pretraining runs remain a case where a one-year commitment really does win. If a cluster is occupied by one large job for weeks without pauses, its utilization is close to 100%, clearly above u*, and the commitment discount works in full. The mixed model does not reject long-term commitments. It only requires that they be applied to the part of the load that deserves them.

Fifth, and perhaps the most important: organizational risk. If nobody owns this decision, meaning there is no person who recalculates the baseline once a month, things fairly quickly return to the familiar "rent with headroom". It is the safest choice for each individual participant and the most expensive for the company as a whole. To prevent this, the decision needs an owner with clear responsibility and a regular update cycle.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
We started with a cluster rented for a year and loaded to a third. Its problem is not the hardware or the provider but that load and cost were not designed. GPU load in model development is bimodal, small jobs use accelerators poorly, and paying the "continuous operation" rate for such a load usually means overpaying.

The alternative is a mixed model. The minimum baseline, loaded above the threshold u*, is covered by a commitment, and everything else is taken on demand or through short-term reservations booked in advance. In the four-node example, this scheme cost $18,945 a month against $64,116 for renting with headroom. This result is not universal, but the method presented lets you compare a node's utilization with the threshold and decide by calculation, not by feel.

Infracost makes this approach practical because it brings cost into the infrastructure development process. When the estimate is visible in the pull request, and budgets and policies guard against accidental decisions, cost becomes as verifiable a property of the system as reliability or security. It is visible before it turns into a bill, and that is the main idea of cost-driven infrastructure.

docs.title: От Jupyter Notebook к промышленной ML-системе
docs.text: Почему 90% моделей никогда не становятся промышленными решениями

docs.title: Введение
docs.text:
История большинства ML-проектов выглядит одинаково.

В Data Science отделе появляется Jupyter Notebook. На тестовых данных модель показывает Accuracy 96%.

Через несколько месяцев оказывается, что модель так и не используется в бизнесе.

Почему?

Потому что модель — это всего лишь одна небольшая деталь системы.

Настоящая ML-система — это десятки сервисов, сотни архитектурных решений и огромное количество инженерных компромиссов.

В этой статье мы пройдем путь от первого ноутбука до промышленной AI-платформы глазами архитектора.

Это стадия исследования.

Основные ошибки

  • Пытаться проектировать Enterprise-архитектуру до появления первой модели.
  • Игнорировать воспроизводимость экспериментов.

Через неделю уже невозможно понять:

  • какая версия данных использовалась;
  • какие параметры обучения были;
  • какая модель дала лучший результат.

Следующий вызов

Ноутбук умеет обучать модель.

Бизнес хочет получать прогнозы автоматически.

Появляется первая архитектурная задача.

docs.title: Этап 2. Первый сервис инференса
docs.text:
• REST API
  • Контейнеризация
  • Версионирование моделей
  • Контроль схем данных

Notebook ↓ Saved Model ↓ REST API ↓ Application

Что изменилось - Теперь модель должна отвечать на запросы.

Она становится частью продукта.

Задачи архитектора

Необходимо решить:

  • как сериализовать модель;
  • где она будет храниться;
  • как загружаться;
  • как обновляться;
  • как масштабироваться.

Появляются:

  • FastAPI
  • MLflow
  • Docker

Главные ошибки

  • Модель загружается на каждый запрос
  • Нет контроля версии модели
  • Нет контроля схемы входных данных
  • API ломается после первого обновления модели

Следующий вызов

Модель работает.

Но как ее переобучать?

docs.title: Этап 3. Автоматизация обучения
docs.text:
• Training Pipeline
  • Registry
  • CI/CD для ML
  • Воспроизводимость

Появляется pipeline.

Data ↓ Validation ↓ Training ↓ Evaluation ↓ Registry

Архитектурные задачи

Архитектор начинает думать уже не о модели.

Он проектирует процесс.

Появляются вопросы:

  • кто запускает обучение;
  • когда запускать обучение;
  • как откатывать неудачные версии;
  • как хранить артефакты;
  • как воспроизводить обучение.

Главные ошибки

Обучение запускается вручную.

Никто не знает:

  • какая модель сейчас используется;
  • почему именно она;
  • можно ли повторить обучение.

docs.title: Этап 4. Данные становятся системой
docs.text:
• Data Platform
  • Feature Store
  • Data Quality
  • Data Contracts

До этого данные были “файлом”.

Теперь это полноценная инфраструктура.

Sources ↓ ETL ↓ Feature Store ↓ Training ↓ Serving

Новые задачи архитектора

Самая большая проблема ML — не модель и не данные.

Необходимо обеспечить:

  • единые признаки;
  • отсутствие data leakage;
  • одинаковую обработку train/inference;
  • контроль качества данных.

Главные ошибки

Feature Engineering реализован два раза.

Один код — для обучения.

Второй — для продакшена.

Через месяц модели начинают расходиться.

docs.title: Этап 5. Появляется Production
docs.text:
• SLA
  • Масштабирование
  • Kubernetes
  • Безопасность

Теперь модель используется пользователями.

Возникают новые требования.

Users ↓ API Gateway ↓ Model Service ↓ Monitoring ↓ Logs

Задачи архитектора

Теперь появляются вопросы:

  • SLA;
  • отказоустойчивость;
  • масштабирование;
  • балансировка;
  • безопасность.

Ошибки

Архитектор думает только о модели.

На практике система падает потому что:

  • закончилось место в очереди;
  • Redis переполнен;
  • API не выдержал нагрузку;
  • Kubernetes пересоздал Pod.

docs.title: Этап 6. Monitoring
docs.text:
• Model Drift
  • Data Drift
  • Concept Drift
  • Бизнес-метрики
  • Observability

Теперь нужно понять — модель вообще работает?

Контролируются уже не только серверы

Теперь необходимо измерять:

  • качество модели;
  • drift;
  • data drift;
  • concept drift;
  • распределение признаков;
  • задержки;
  • стоимость инференса.

Главная ошибка

Следить только за CPU и RAM.

Модель может работать идеально… но ее качество уже упало в два раза.

docs.title: Этап 7. Continuous Learning
docs.text:
• Автоматическое переобучение
  • Canary Deployment
  • Shadow Deployment

Модель постепенно устаревает.

Необходимо организовать цикл жизни.

Production ↓ Monitoring ↓ Retraining ↓ Validation ↓ Canary ↓ Production

Вопросы архитектора

  • Как сравнить новую модель со старой?

  • Как откатиться назад?

Ошибки

  • Без понимания, стало ли лучше.

  • безопасность;
  • стандарты;

Основные вызовы

  • Zero Trust;
  • RBAC/ABAC;

  • GitOps;

docs.title: From Jupyter Notebook to a Production ML System
docs.text: Why Successful ML Models Still Fail to Become Production Systems

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The story of most ML projects is remarkably repetitive. A Jupyter notebook appears in the data science department. The model shows 98% accuracy on a test set, management is impressed, and the project is declared a success. A few months pass, and it turns out the model never left the notebook: the business isn't using it, it isn't generating revenue, and it is gradually forgotten along with the virtual environment it was trained in — even though its creation consumed months of engineering time. What remains, in the end, is sunk cost. The problem isn't that the model was bad — its metrics proved it worked. The problem is that the cost of moving it into a production loop turned out to be far too high.

Industry experience, accumulated over many years, shows that only a small fraction of models developed in research mode ever reach production — a figure repeated so often in the professional community that it has become something of an aphorism. The reason isn't the quality of the models or the competence of the data scientists; the reason is that a model is only one small part of a much larger system. Google's now-classic paper "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" demonstrated this most vividly: the model code itself occupies only a small fraction of the overall architecture, surrounded by a mass of infrastructure components — data verification, feature extraction, serving infrastructure, monitoring, and dozens of others, each accumulating its own technical debt [6].

A real ML system isn't a model — it's dozens of services, architectural decisions, and an enormous amount of engineering work. The path from the first experiment to a production AI platform is rarely a straight line, but it almost always passes through the same stages of maturation. In this article, we'll walk that path through the eyes of an architect — from a Jupyter notebook to a platform that unifies classical machine learning, LLMs, and AI agents.

The nine stages described below aren't a rigid methodology or a standard — they're a generalization of a recurring pattern seen in companies of every size, from a startup with a single model to a corporation running dozens of teams. Some organizations move through these stages in a few months; others stretch the transition over years; still others compress several adjacent stages into a single sprint. But the order in which the architectural questions arise is surprisingly stable: first you have to prove the model works at all, and only then that it can work reliably, reproducibly, and at scale. Trying to reverse that order — designing an enterprise platform before a single working model exists — is a classic case of over-engineering: it burns time building architecture for requirements that aren't yet known.

docs.title: Stage 1. The Jupyter Notebook
docs.text:
At the start there isn't much: a notebook, a dataset, and a trained model. Formally, everything works — you can run the cells top to bottom and get a prediction.

CSV -> Pandas -> Notebook -> Model

This is the stage of pure research, and its value shouldn't be underestimated: it's where the basic hypothesis gets tested — can the model solve the problem at all?

At this stage, there is no architect as such. There's a researcher, whose main job is to prove the idea works and holds up on real data. Any attempt to design an architecture before a working model exists is effort spent on a problem that doesn't yet exist. The path from Python code in a notebook to a production-grade ML system begins precisely by recognizing that this stage calls not for architecture, but for experimental discipline [2].

The most common mistake here is ignoring the reproducibility of experiments. After a week of active work, it's already impossible to reconstruct which version of the data was used, which hyperparameters produced the best result, or why one model was chosen over another. This is where the first layer of the hidden technical debt that Sculley and co-authors describe gets laid down: the confusion between code, data, and configuration doesn't arise in production — it arises right here, during uncontrolled experimentation [6].

It's worth dispelling a common misconception here: reproducibility at the notebook stage isn't about Docker or pipelines — it's about basic discipline. Fixing a seed, saving the dataset version, and logging the hyperparameters and metrics of every run is enough to avoid having to reconstruct the logic of an experiment from memory a month later. The absence of this discipline isn't critical as long as the model lives in the head of a single researcher, but it becomes costly the moment other people join the process at the next stage.

One common solution at this stage is adopting an ML experiment tracking system — MLflow, Weights & Biases, DVC, or something similar. Doing so is a sign of a researcher's maturity and their intent to keep the experiment at the right standard. These systems let you track hyperparameters, datasets, and model metrics, and to store and retrieve the best model by a chosen metric. Using one can be extremely valuable even for a single engineer, and becomes essential the moment more than one person starts working on the model.

A notebook can train a model, but the business wants predictions delivered automatically, not on request from a data scientist. This is where the first genuinely architectural task appears: how to expose the model's output to the outside world.

docs.title: Stage 2. The First Inference Service
docs.text:
The model stops being a research artifact and becomes part of the product — it now has to answer requests in real time.

Notebook -> Saved Model -> REST API -> Application

The first real circuit of architectural decisions appears: how to serialize the model, where to store it, how to load it when the service starts, how to update it without downtime, and how to scale it under load. The typical stack at this stage is FastAPI for serving requests, MLflow for tracking and versioning the model, and Docker for packaging the environment. Practical experience building a fully automated CI/CD pipeline on top of MLflow, GitHub Actions, FastAPI, and Docker illustrates well what even a minimal production wrapper around a model consists of [1]. It's also worth noting that changing the model is only one of three axes of change in an ML system, alongside code and data; the CD4ML methodology explicitly states that all three axes need to be versioned and deployed reproducibly at the same time [8].

The most common problem at this stage is a model that gets reloaded on every single request, which kills the service's performance. Close behind are the absence of model version control, the absence of input schema validation, and, as a consequence, an API that breaks after the very first model update because nobody warned consumers that the contract had changed.

The question of the data contract deserves special attention. Real, often messy traffic from external systems now hits the service's input — not a neatly prepared test dataset. Without an explicit input schema, the model will sooner or later receive a request it was never trained for, and will either return a meaningless prediction or crash on an unhandled exception. Even at this stage, it makes sense to build basic input validation as a separate layer ahead of the model call, rather than as part of the model's own code.

This stage typically marks the transition from a model in a Jupyter notebook to code organized as separate classes. The data preprocessor, the training code, the inference code, input/output validation, and error handling all split apart. The code stops being a research notebook where the order in which cells are executed affects the result, and takes on the character of a finished project ready for automation.

Request and response handling is introduced, and the first data contract takes shape.

The model works and answers requests. But the next question arises: how do you retrain it as new data appears?

docs.title: Stage 3. Training Automation
docs.text:
Manual training runs give way to a pipeline — a reproducible sequence of steps from raw data to a registered model.

Data -> Validation -> Training -> Evaluation -> Registry

At this stage we stop thinking of the model as a single artifact and start designing a process. This is where the role of "architect" first emerges — someone who begins to make sense of what's happening and to plan how to embed the resulting microservice into the existing system, or how to design a new one around it.

Questions start to arise: who runs training and when, how do you roll back to a previous version in case of regression, where are training artifacts stored, and how do you guarantee that training can be reproduced a month or a year from now?

Google Cloud formalizes this transition through its MLOps maturity model: level 0 is a manual, fully human-driven process; level 1 adds continuous model training control through an automated pipeline; and level 2 includes full CI/CD for the ML pipeline itself, including data validation at every step [7]. The CD4ML methodology describes the same requirements slightly differently — as the need to make model training a deterministic, repeatable step in a single delivery pipeline, rather than a one-off action performed by a researcher [8].

If training is still triggered manually, the team inevitably loses visibility: nobody can say for certain which model is currently running in production, why that particular model was chosen, or whether the training process that produced it can even be repeated.

The model registry deserves its own mention here — a component that, at this stage, stops being a convenient file store and becomes the source of truth for which model version is used where and why. It's the registry that ties together the training metadata (which data, which code, which metrics), the model artifact itself, and its promotion status across stages, from staging to production. Without that link, the registry degenerates into a dumping ground of files named things like model_final_v2_new.pkl, which undoes all the effort put into automation.

The pipeline trains the model reproducibly. But where does the pipeline get its data from, and can that data's quality be trusted?

docs.title: Stage 4. Data Becomes a System
docs.text:
Up to this point, data was just a file. Now it's full-fledged infrastructure with its own components and owners.

Sources -> ETL -> Feature Store -> Training -> Serving

Here the architect runs into what is arguably the most underestimated problem in machine learning — not the model, not the volume of data, but the consistency of features between training and inference. You need a single set of features shared by training and serving, no leakage of the target variable, identical data-processing logic in both loops, and continuous quality control over incoming data. It's precisely to solve this problem that the industry developed the Feature Store pattern — a shared feature repository accessible both to the training pipeline and to the inference service.

The emergence of managed platforms such as Google Vertex AI, with a dedicated Feature Store as one of their central components, is direct confirmation that this problem is systemic rather than isolated [5]. Sculley and co-authors separately emphasize that it's data, not code, that is the source of the most invisible and most expensive forms of technical debt in ML systems — through hidden feedback loops and undocumented dependencies between data sources [6].

The classic mistake at this stage is duplicating feature engineering: the same logic, with small variations, gets written twice — once for training, once for production. After a month in operation, these two implementations inevitably diverge, and the model in production starts behaving differently from the model that was validated on historical data.

Data contracts are another element that shifts, at this stage, from optional practice to necessity. The team that produces data (a transactional system, say, or a frontend event system) and the team that consumes it for model training rarely sit within the same circle of responsibility. If the data format or the semantics of a field change without warning — and in practice this happens routinely — the training pipeline either fails outright or, worse, keeps running and trains the model on corrupted data. An explicit contract, captured as a schema and validated automatically at the ETL entry point, turns this hidden dependency into a managed, observable process.

So: the data is organized, the features are consistent. But the model still serves only a limited number of test requests — what happens once real users start relying on it?

docs.title: Stage 5. Production Arrives
docs.text:
The model goes live for real users, and with that comes an entirely new class of requirements — not about prediction quality, but about service reliability.

Users -> API Gateway -> Model Service -> Monitoring -> Logs

The focus now shifts to SLAs (Service Level Agreements), fault tolerance, horizontal scaling, load balancing, and access security. The inference service stops being a standalone application and becomes part of the company's broader production infrastructure, with its typical control plane, serving plane, and observability plane, deployed on managed compute and orchestrated through Kubernetes with proper user access control [1].

The most painful mistake at this stage is viewing system reliability purely through the lens of model quality. In practice, production systems fail for entirely different reasons: a message queue runs out of space, a cache fills up, an API can't handle a traffic spike, or Kubernetes recreates the pod running the model at the worst possible moment, wiping out a warmed-up cache.

Infrastructure matters more than the model

At the production stage, infrastructure decisions — not algorithmic ones — most often determine the quality of the system and whether it survives real load. An architect who keeps optimizing accuracy instead of p99 latency and fault tolerance at this stage is solving the wrong problem.

The service is stable and serving real traffic. But is the model actually delivering the value it was expected to?

docs.title: Stage 6. Monitoring
docs.text:
At this stage, it's no longer just servers that come under scrutiny. The central question shifts: not "is the service available," but "is the model still actually useful."

You now have to measure model quality over time, track model drift, data drift, and concept drift, monitor the distribution of input features, watch response latency, and even track the cost of a single inference call. Google Cloud explicitly ties this discipline to the earlier maturity stages: without continuous training, without input data validation, and without model drift monitoring, a process simply cannot be called production-grade [7]. In an ecosystem built around MLflow and containerized serving, observability is typically implemented through Prometheus and Grafana on top of a dedicated monitoring dashboard that collects metrics separately from the service's business logic [1].

The most common — and most expensive — mistake at this stage is watching only CPU and memory. A model can respond in milliseconds and produce zero infrastructure-level errors, while its real-world quality on new data has already dropped by half, and the business won't notice until, at best, the next quarterly report.

It's important to distinguish between three types of drift that need to be tracked simultaneously.

Data drift is a change in the distribution of input features relative to what the model was trained on — for example, the age profile of shoppers changes in an online store.

Concept drift is a trickier problem: the relationship between the features and the target variable itself changes over time, even if the input distribution stays the same.

Model drift is the umbrella term for an observed drop in model quality, regardless of which of the first two causes triggered it. Without distinguishing between these, a team typically reacts to the symptom rather than the cause, and retrains the model when what actually needs to change is the feature set.

Degradation is caught in time. The next question is how to respond to it without manual intervention every single time.

docs.title: Stage 7. Continuous Learning
docs.text:
Every model gradually becomes outdated as the world around it changes, so it needs a full lifecycle built around it — one closed into a continuous loop.

Production -> Monitoring -> Retraining -> Validation -> Canary -> Production

Here a different order of questions arises: how do you know it's time to retrain, how do you properly compare a new model version against the old one, how do you safely switch users over to it, and how do you roll back quickly if something goes wrong?

To switch safely, the industry uses canary deployment and shadow deployment — gradually rolling the new model out to a portion of traffic, or running it in parallel without affecting users at all, which lets you compare metrics before a full release. This is a direct continuation of the continuous-training principles Google Cloud describes [7], and of CD4ML's ideas about continuous, reproducible, and safely reversible delivery of model changes [8].

The most common mistake is retraining "on a schedule" — once a week or once a month — without any real understanding of whether the new model actually improved on the previous one, or whether the retraining was worth the resources spent on it at all. This approach creates the illusion of automation without answering the one question that matters: did the retraining actually help?

The difference between canary and shadow deployment is often a source of confusion in practice, even though it's fundamental. In a canary deployment, a portion of real traffic is genuinely routed to the new model, and its mistakes are visible to users — the risk is offset by keeping that traffic share small and tightly controlled. In a shadow deployment, the new model receives a copy of the traffic in parallel with the old one, but its responses are never shown to users — only logged for comparison — which lets you evaluate the new version with zero risk, though it tells you nothing about how users would actually react to it. A mature platform typically uses both patterns in sequence: shadow first, to gather statistics, then canary, to roll out gradually into live operation.

The lifecycle of a single model is now in place. But what happens when there isn't just one model anymore, but hundreds — and not one team managing them, but dozens?

docs.title: Stage 8. Enterprise ML Platform
docs.text:
Once an organization has hundreds of models and dozens of teams building them, one-off solutions stop scaling. They're replaced by a platform with shared services: identity, projects, feature store, registry, pipelines, serving, monitoring, security, cost control, and governance.

The architect's role now takes on a central function: they design not a model, not even a single service, but the platform itself, its processes, team structure, security standards, and the operating cost of the whole enterprise.

The focus shifts to multi-tenancy, so that different teams can safely share common infrastructure; GitOps as the single way changes get delivered; Zero Trust and RBAC/ABAC access models; reproducibility at the level of the entire platform; and compliance and FinOps.

The emergence of managed platforms at the level of Google Vertex AI — unifying Feature Store, Experiments, Pipelines, and Continuous Monitoring in a single ecosystem — is essentially industrial confirmation that this exact set of services is what an organization operating ML at scale actually needs [5]. Governance stops being a formality at this stage: the experience of government programs such as the Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand, where more than twenty government agencies voluntarily committed to transparent, accountable, and fair use of algorithms with the support of a dedicated Data Ethics Advisory Group, shows that governance isn't bureaucratic overhead — it's a necessary element of a mature platform, especially where model decisions directly affect people [3].

The main danger here is trying to solve organizational and process problems purely with technical means — scaling up infrastructure without changing access-management processes, quality standards, or accountability for the decisions the model makes.

The platform can now serve classical ML models at industrial scale. But the industry has already posed the next question to the architect: how do you fold large language models and agents into this same platform?

docs.title: Stage 9. AI Platform
docs.text:
The next level of maturity goes beyond classical machine learning. Large language models, RAG, AI agents, the MCP protocol, vector databases, orchestration, state machines, and policy engines all get added to the familiar set of components.

Businesses today increasingly see generative AI not as a threat, but as a source of productivity growth — this shift in business sentiment toward AI is directly noted in the business press covering companies adopting generative models [4]. It's exactly this demand that pushes the architect beyond the traditional ML stack. Now they're designing not a standalone ML system, but an intelligent enterprise platform, where LLMs and AI agents aren't isolated experiments but full-fledged components of the overall architecture, subject to the same principles of versioning, observability, and governance developed at earlier stages.

The mistake at this stage mirrors the mistake of the first one: just as a Jupyter notebook gets pushed into production without any architecture around it, LLMs and agents are often bolted onto the platform without bringing along the discipline of prompt versioning, token cost control, and generation quality monitoring — repeating, in effect, a journey classical ML already took ten years to complete.

Here, the evolutionary cycle of the architecture doesn't end — it begins again, at a new level of complexity, but following the same principles.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The central idea of this article is simple: each stage follows logically from the one before it — it doesn't appear by accident or by fashion. An architect who skips a stage — say, trying to build an Enterprise Platform without working Monitoring in place — is usually forced to return to the skipped level later, but now under the pressure of a production incident rather than at the calm pace of deliberate design.

Stage The architect's central question Notebook Does the idea even work? Inference API How do you deliver a prediction to the user? Training Pipeline How do you reproduce training? Data Platform How do you guarantee data quality? Production How do you ensure service reliability? Monitoring How do you know the model has degraded? Continuous Learning How do you improve the model automatically? Enterprise Platform How do you scale development across dozens of teams? AI Platform How do you unify classical ML, LLMs, and AI agents into a single architecture?

A model that shows impressive accuracy in a notebook is only the beginning of the journey, not the finish line. Between an experiment and a production system stand nine stages of architectural maturation, and most models never reach production precisely because someone tries to skip over one or more of them.

The architect's job isn't to artificially speed up this path, but to walk it deliberately — knowing, at every step, which question needs to be answered next.

Bottom line

The path from a Jupyter notebook to an AI platform isn't a linear checklist — it's a sequence of architectural decisions, each one becoming the foundation for the next.
